title_page_text: The Technology Strategy Board (TSB) is establishing a Connected Digital Economy Catapult to address the challenges of maximising the economic value of the growing digital economy to UK businesses.

The TSB is inviting organisations to register their interest in helping them to establish the Catapult and develop its programme.  Click here to download the Call for Registration of Interest document (PDF, 286KB). The deadline for submitting your details is noon on 28 March 2012. It’s important for Manchester businesses to get their views across – and there will be a process of engagement and consultation from April to June that will give a further opportunity to reflect Manchester’s importance in any national programme.

If you would like to be kept abreast of developments, receive event notifications and discuss the Catapult with the TSB, they strongly recommend you join the SIG on https://connect.innovateuk.org/web/connected-digital-economy.
You can also follow @Catapult_TSB on Twitter, or follow the public list  created for the Digital Connected Economy Catapult.

Market opportunity

title_page_text: DRAFT
Creative Industries
Fostering innovation and growth across the digital economy
April 2012
1	Introduction

This document seeks to inform discussions regarding the development of a new Catapult for the Connected Digital Economy (CDEC), as proposed by the Technology Strategy Board. Building on consultation undertaken across the creative sector, it highlights the major innovation challenges being faced by creative businesses and raises issues of direct relevance to the CDEC proposal.
In particular, it focuses on the contribution that small creative businesses can make to the challenges being faced by businesses across the broader digital economy.
2	Context

The UK’s creative industries have an established international reputation for driving innovation in product, services, content and experience. The 13 Creative Industries sectors, ranging from advertising to video games, are of significant economic size – 6.4%% of GVA, with over 182,000 companies accounting for 1.3 million employees and £17.3bn of exports annually. In addition, the creative industries are critical to the success of a number of inter-connected UK industries, such as manufacturing, leisure, tourism and, of course, digital technologies. If we were able to encourage closer collaboration between the UK’s content and technology sectors, the opportunity for growth in the ‘digital economy’ would be considerable. If sectors representing roughly 5% of GVA (ICT) were pulling together with another 6.4% of GVA, the outcome could be truly transformative.
3	The Challenge

Consultation undertaken by the Creative Industries KTN in 2011 suggested that the UK’s creative industries are at a crossroads: one path leading through convergence with technology to a digital economy of considerable size and international reputation, the other to the slow erosion of economic value and international standing as competitors from both established and emerging economies take the lead. This cross-roads is illustrated by the way innovation in content sectors such as music, publishing, video games and TV is being driven by our global competitors.  As the new global content delivery platforms (Apple's iPad and iTunes, Amazon's Kindle and Sony's PS3) are being created elsewhere, so the lion's share of the ensuing value chain will also be extracted elsewhere. At the same time, the essential production tools creative industries depend upon are almost all developed elsewhere.

Given this, urgent action is required to support innovation.  In particular we need to address the challenge of ensuring creative businesses take up, exploit and drive the relevant technologies coming through university research.  Equally, we need to create opportunities and environments where businesses from different sectors in the creative industries can come together to collaborate and innovate.
4	Convergence

Critical to the competitive future of the UK’s digital economy is the ways in which digital communication technologies can improve the functioning of the overall Creative Industries value chain, rather than simply the individual elements within it. From content creation and production, to distribution and consumption – what was once a clear and definable linear process is becoming converged, contested and dis-intermediated.

This convergence is disrupting existing value chains, transforming traditional business models and creating new markets. Although in certain sectors, disintermediation and the dismantling of the value chain may well be an outcome, it is by no means inevitable. Rather, there is an opportunity in all of the value chain elements to use digital technologies to genuinely add value, so that the role of intermediaries (e.g. broadcasters, publishers, distributors) is an enriched one, acting much more than simply as a gateway-keeper or route to market.

title_page_text: Working draft
Creative Industries
Fostering innovation and growth across the digital economy
April 2012
1	Introduction and Context

This document seeks to inform discussions regarding the development of a new Catapult for the Connected Digital Economy (CDEC), as proposed by the Technology Strategy Board. Building on consultation being undertaken by the TSB, it highlights the major innovation challenges being faced by creative and digital businesses. In so doing it recognises that there are wider legislative and regulatory debates, for instance around developing an appropriate IP framework for the UK, but the focus is around what could practically be achieved by the CDEC itself, particularly on strengthening the contribution that small creative businesses can make to the challenges being faced across the broader digital economy.

The UK’s creative industries have an established international reputation for driving innovation in product, services, content and experience. The 13 Creative Industries sectors, ranging from advertising to video games, are of significant economic size – 6.4% of GVA, with over 182,000 companies accounting for 1.3 million employees and £17.3bn of exports annually. In addition, the creative industries are critical to the success of a number of inter-connected UK industries, such as manufacturing, leisure, tourism and, of course, digital technologies. If we were able to encourage closer collaboration between the UK’s content and technology sectors, the opportunity for growth in the ‘digital economy’ would be considerable. If sectors representing roughly 5% of GVA (ICT) were pulling together with another 6.4% of GVA, the outcome could be truly transformative.
2	The Challenge

Consultation undertaken by the Creative Industries KTN in 2011 suggested that the UK’s creative industries are at a crossroads: one path leading through convergence with technology to a digital economy of considerable size and international reputation, the other to the slow erosion of economic value and international standing as competitors from both established and emerging economies take the lead. This cross-roads is illustrated by the way innovation in content sectors such as music, publishing, video games and TV is being driven by our global competitors.  As the new global content delivery platforms (Apple's iPad and iTunes, Amazon's Kindle and Sony's PS3) are being created elsewhere, so the lion's share of the ensuing value chain will also be extracted elsewhere. At the same time, many of the essential production tools creative industries depend upon are almost all developed elsewhere.

Critical to understanding the competitive future of the UK’s digital economy is the manner in which digital communication technologies are impacting on the overall Creative Industries value chain, rather than simply the individual elements within it. From content creation and production, to distribution and consumption – what was once a clear and definable linear process is becoming converged, contested and dis-intermediated. This convergence is disrupting existing value chains, transforming traditional business models and creating new markets. Although much industry discussion is focused around the by-passing and dismantling of the value chain, there is an opportunity in all of the value chain elements to use digital technologies to genuinely add value, so that the role of intermediaries (e.g. broadcasters, publishers, distributors) is an enriched one, acting much more than simply as a gateway-keeper or route to market. For example, by speeding up the time it takes new products and services to come to market; encouraging collaboration, joint research and commercial partnerships between businesses and organisations; or by added functionality provided by different parts of the value chain through a metadata-embedded product/service.

Although circumstances will be depend upon the sector and where one resides within the value chain, for those operating in the creative and digital economy we can identify a number of over-arching challenges that all businesses are currently facing:
Fast pace of economic change
Need for new apps and services
Better understanding of the consumer, and changing consumer trends
The need to respond quickly and flexibly to market conditions and opportunities
